item.title: Adoption is outrunning governance
item.description:
AI agents have reached the largest companies faster than the rules for running them. By Microsoft’s own telemetry, more than 80% of Fortune 500 companies use active AI agents built with low-code or no-code tools.1 Four recent surveys measure how far governance trails that spread. They ask different questions of different people, so each one needs to be read on its own terms.

Each survey measures something different

In the table below, the middle column shows how far agents have spread in each study, and the last column shows what has not kept pace with them.

Four studies of AI agents, each read on its own terms
Study How far agents have spread What lags behind
Deloitte, State of AI in the Enterprise 2026, a survey of 3,235 business and IT leaders in 24 countries2 Close to three-quarters of companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years Only 21% of the companies planning to deploy report a mature model for agent governance
KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse, third quarter of 2026, a survey of 314 US leaders at companies with revenue of $1 billion or more3 62% of organizations are building, deploying or developing AI agents 49% have set boundaries where agents may not make decisions on their own
Microsoft Cyber Pulse, February 2026, from Microsoft’s telemetry and a survey it commissioned of more than 1,700 data security professionals1 More than 80% of Fortune 500 companies use active AI agents built with low-code or no-code tools 29% of employees have turned to unsanctioned AI agents for work tasks
BCG, The Widening AI Value Gap, September 20254 AI agents’ share of the value AI creates is expected to rise from about 17% in 2025 to 29% by 2028 Only 5% of companies are “future-built” for AI, and 60% report hardly any material value

The four results can’t be added up or charted as one trend, because their samples differ in country, company size and date, and each study counts something different. Deloitte counted plans to deploy,2 KPMG counted organizations building or running agents,3 Microsoft measured agents in active use,1 and BCG estimated where the value of AI will come from.4

Read one at a time, the studies still point the same way. In each one, the measure of adoption runs ahead of the measure of control, whether that control is a governance model, a boundary on what agents may decide alone, or a rule against tools nobody approved.

Companies sense the gap in their own operations. In Deloitte’s 2026 technology predictions, 80% of organizations consider their basic automation mature, but only 28% say so once AI agents are included.5 The cost of leaving the gap open shows up in forecasts. Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls.6 Each of those causes is something a control plane exists to manage, which is why the controls need to be in place before the next wave of agents arrives.

What to do next

  1. CIO. Ask for a list of every agent in use, including those built with low-code tools, with a named owner for each.
  2. CTO. Route agent actions through one policy enforcement point, so each rule is written once and applied to every agent, whichever vendor built it.
  3. CIO and CTO. Agree autonomy tiers before the next rollout. Each agent’s tier should set what it may do alone and what needs a person’s approval.

Go deeper

Section 1 of The AI Control Plane Handbook sets these surveys beside an integration benchmark and an analyst forecast, and explains why coordinating models and agents has become an infrastructure problem. Slide 4 of the executive deck puts the four results on one page, with speaker notes you can present from.

Try it

Before you quote figures like these, Quote a survey figure with its weights and margin of error shows what to check first, with a notebook you can run in Colab.

item.title: What an enterprise AI control plane is
item.description:
The hyperscalers now describe their agent platforms as control planes, and Microsoft calls Agent 365 “the control-plane for AI agents.”1 A label that every vendor can claim helps a buyer only when it means something that can be tested. A short definition and three capabilities give it that meaning, and each capability turns into a question to ask before anyone signs a contract.

A definition with edges

A Deloitte Insights analysis from August 2026 defines an enterprise control plane as a governed, intelligent layer that mediates decisions across systems, deciding who can act, what data can be accessed, how workloads execute and how AI agents operate within defined cost, latency and regulatory boundaries.2 It resembles service-oriented architecture, but it is event-driven and does more than expose reusable services, because it coordinates workflows as conditions change.

HCLTech’s April 2026 analysis suggests judging a platform by what it governs as well as by what it does, since control planes compete for authority more than for attention.3 The same analysis observes that an agent without identity constraints is automation without accountability.3

Three capabilities turn the definition into questions

Deloitte’s analysis rests the control plane on three capabilities.2 Each decides something different, and each can be put to a vendor as a single question.

The three capabilities of an AI control plane, with the question each one answers
Capability What it decides The question to ask
Architecture Whether enterprise capabilities can be exposed securely and flexibly across channels, agents, clouds, edge and on-premises systems Can agents safely reach what the business can do?
Orchestration Which model and agent handle a task, where it runs and under which constraints Which model and agent should handle this task, and where?
Trust, security and resilience Identity, authority, integrity and control across every human and machine interaction Can we prove who acted, on whose authority, and why?

A product that answers one question well can still leave the other two open. A catalog of connectors speaks to architecture, a model router speaks to orchestration, and an audit dashboard speaks to trust, yet none of them alone decides who may act on what, which is why the definition asks for all three in one governed layer.

A good answer to each question is something a vendor can show on your own systems:

  • Architecture. One real business capability, such as checking an order’s status, exposed as a governed API or tool that an agent reaches with its own identity and its own limits.
  • Orchestration. One task routed to a model and an agent by rules you can read, covering cost, latency and where the data may go.
  • Trust. The record of one completed action, naming the agent, the person it acted for, the policy that allowed it and the approval, if one was needed.

Most enterprises span several ecosystems, so the harder task is coordinating control planes across them. That is the case for a vendor-neutral control plane, one that keeps identity, policy and audit in a layer the enterprise owns while models and agents come from many sources.

What to do next

  1. CIO. Put the three questions into your next platform review, and ask each vendor to answer them on one of your own use cases.
  2. CTO. Map today’s stack against the three capabilities, product by product, and mark each question that no product answers yet.
  3. Architect. Check that identity, policy and audit records sit in a layer you would keep if you changed model or agent vendors.

Go deeper

Section 2 of The AI Control Plane Handbook sets out the definition and the lifecycle a control plane enforces for every agent, from proposal to retirement. Slide 7 of the executive deck puts the three capabilities and their questions on one page.

item.title: Builders need to plan for the 2026 changes to MCP and A2A
item.description:
Agents reach tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and reach other agents through the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A), and both changed substantially in 2026. The pace is already a problem for the people who build on them, and in the 2026 Connectivity Benchmark, 68% of IT leaders said they find it hard to keep up with emerging agent standards and protocols.1

Where each change lands

MCP standardizes how agents reach tools and data,2 and A2A standardizes how agents collaborate.3 Both are now projects of the Agentic AI Foundation, hosted by the Linux Foundation.2,3 A third protocol, for agent payments, is moving the same way.

Three agent protocols that changed in 2026
Protocol What changed in 2026 Where it lands
A2A Version 1.0, the first stable release, arrived in March 2026 with version negotiation, multi-tenancy and signed agent cards that let one agent verify another’s identity3 Any agent that accepts work from another agent
MCP The July 2026 revision made the protocol stateless, removing sessions and the initialization handshake, and requires headers that name the method and tool on every HTTP request2 Every MCP server that held session state, and every gateway that reads MCP traffic
AP2 Google contributed its Agent Payments Protocol to the FIDO Alliance in April 2026, where new working groups are developing standards for agent authentication and agent-initiated payments4 Any agent that can start a payment

The MCP revision did more than remove state. It documents how OpenTelemetry trace context travels with each call, tightens authorization checks and deprecates several features with a minimum 12-month window.2 That window is the deadline for any tool that still relies on a deprecated feature. Agent payments are at an earlier stage, and until the new standards are settled, AP2 is best treated as pre-standard.

For MCP, statelessness means every request carries what the server needs, and no server keeps a session between calls. A server can then run behind an ordinary load balancer, since no request depends on an earlier one. For A2A, an agent card is the description an agent publishes of itself, and a signature lets another agent check who published it before it trusts the work on offer.

The cost of each change depends on how agent traffic is wired. Where every agent connects to every tool on its own, each team re-implements each change in its own code and on its own schedule, and the slowest team sets the pace for everyone. A control plane absorbs much of that work in one place. Its registry can check signed agent cards before one agent trusts another, and its gateway can apply policy to MCP’s standard headers and join every call to its trace, so a change to the protocol becomes a change to one policy, and the same traces show which tools still call a deprecated feature as the window closes.

What to do next

  1. Developer. List every MCP server you run, and check which ones still hold session state or leave out the method and tool headers, starting with the servers your production agents call most.
  2. AI Engineer. Require a signed agent card before an agent accepts work from another agent, and give no privilege to roles an agent asserts about itself.
  3. Developer and AI Engineer. Track the MCP deprecations against their 12-month window, and keep any payment flow built on AP2 behind a person’s approval while the standards work continues.

Go deeper

Section 4 of The AI Control Plane Handbook places the protocols inside a control plane’s routing, context engineering and delegation. Slide 13 of the executive deck sets the protocols beside context engineering and capability discovery.

item.title: Each OWASP agentic threat maps to a control you can test
item.description:
Security teams judge any agent platform against the threat lists they already use. For agents, the list is the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, published in December 2025, which names ten risks specific to AI agents.1 Every one of the ten maps to controls a team can put in place and test now.

Every risk on the list has a control

The table maps each risk to the controls that address it in an AI control plane.

Ten agentic risks from OWASP, with the controls that address each in the author’s mapping1
Agentic risk What it looks like Controls
ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack Hidden instructions in content, documents or tool results redirect the agent’s goal Input and tool-result screening at the gateway
Allow-listed tools per agent
Approvals bound to the exact action
ASI02 Tool Misuse A legitimate tool is used in a harmful way Per-agent tool allow-lists
Schema validation
Rate, spend and exposure limits
ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse Leaked or inherited credentials let an agent act beyond its scope One identity per agent
Short-lived, task-scoped tokens
Delegation that narrows
Real-time revocation
ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities Poisoned tools, MCP servers, plugins or models enter at runtime Only registered, signed and version-pinned MCP servers are callable
A private registry of trusted servers
An agent bill of materials2
ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution Natural-language paths trigger code or commands Sandboxed execution
Code and shell tools only at an explicit tier
Limits on outbound connections
ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning Poisoned memory or context shapes later decisions Context only from governed sources (master data, catalog, lineage)
Provenance checks
Session integrity monitoring
ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication Spoofed or altered messages between agents Signed agent cards
Mutual authentication
A2A traffic through the gateway
No privilege from self-asserted roles
ASI08 Cascading Failures Errors spread through automated pipelines Circuit breakers
Cumulative exposure limits across agents and sessions
Propose-only on stale data
ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation Confident, polished output leads people to approve harmful actions Approvals bound to the exact action and showing the facts behind it
Approver drills
Limits that guard against consent fatigue
ASI10 Rogue Agents Agents act outside their mandate or hide what they do Registry and scanners
Honeytokens and decoy tools
Behavioral monitoring
The kill switch

Several controls appear in more than one row, and they are the place to start. Approvals bound to the exact action defend against goal hijack and against people trusting a confident draft. One identity per agent, with delegation that narrows at each hop, closes off privilege abuse and limits what a spoofed message between agents can do. Exposure limits that add up across agents and sessions contain both tool misuse and cascading failures.

The threat lists keep growing. Microsoft’s AI Red Team added seven agentic failure modes to its taxonomy in June 2026, among them agentic supply chain compromise, inter-agent trust escalation, session context contamination and MCP and plugin abuse.3 MITRE ATLAS has added agent-specific techniques since December 2025, such as AI Agent Tool Credential Harvesting and Publish Poisoned AI Agent Tool.4 Tagging red-team scenarios with these names lets a team’s results map to the vocabulary other teams use.

What to do next

  1. Developer. Allow-list the tools each agent may call, validate every call against the tool’s schema, and accept only registered, signed and version-pinned MCP servers.
  2. AI Engineer. Bind each approval to the exact action and show the approver the facts behind it, so a polished draft can’t carry a harmful change through.
  3. CISO. Name an owner for what enters the agent registry and another for what approvers are shown, because no gateway closes either risk alone, and tag red-team scenarios with the risk names in the table.

Go deeper

Section 5 of The AI Control Plane Handbook covers identity for agents, runtime controls, cryptography and human takeover after the kill switch. Slide 17 of the executive deck puts the ten risks and their controls on one page.

item.title: Phase the work so value shows at every milestone
item.description:
Finance will judge an AI control plane program against published payback data, and that data sets a long horizon. In Deloitte’s 2025 survey of 1,854 executives in Europe and the Middle East, most achieved satisfactory ROI on a typical AI use case within two to four years, against the seven to 12 months expected of technology investments.1 A program that phases its work can show value well inside that horizon, one milestone at a time.

Each milestone has value and evidence

The handbook’s plan runs for 24 months in four phases. Each phase ends in a milestone the business can see, with evidence to report at every steering review.

Value delivered and evidence to report at each milestone of a 24-month plan
Milestone Value delivered Evidence to report
Month 3, one front door Every known agent registered with an owner and a tier
Model and tool spend visible by use case
Duplicate and unused agents retired
The first use-case slice live in assist mode		 Agent coverage
Governed traffic
Baseline cost per outcome
The first slice’s KPIs against baseline
Month 8, reusable capabilities New agents reuse governed APIs and MCP tools in place of new integrations
Routine tasks move to lower-cost models within token limits
Use cases scale beyond the pilot		 Reuse of published capabilities
Cost per outcome trend
Run-rate value of live slices against plan
Month 14, trusted autonomy Agents act in systems of record under approvals bound to each action, which is where most of each business case sits
Use-case KPI targets met by month 12
Incidents contained in minutes		 Oversight coverage and effectiveness
Time to contain
Evaluation pass rate
Use-case KPIs at target
Month 24, north star reached All goals met
Use cases at full run rate and sustained
New use cases start on shared controls at lower cost and risk
Models swappable without application changes
Post-quantum migration on track		 The full scorecard at target
Cumulative value against each business case

The architecture delivers value of its own before any use case reaches full scale, from spend visibility at month 3 to faster delivery of every new agent at month 8. Each milestone also brings more of a real use case into production, starting with a first slice that works in assist mode and moving to agents that act in systems of record once the controls are in place.

Expectations of AI payback are shortening. In KPMG’s 2025 Global CEO Outlook, 67% of 1,350 CEOs expected returns on AI within one to three years, where a year earlier most expected three to five.2 Google Cloud’s 2026 survey of 2,403 executives found 84% seeing increasing financial returns from AI and 26% seeing returns accelerate year over year.3 Phasing lets a program beat the two-to-four-year benchmark, because read-only and propose-only slices release capacity within months and help fund the controls that the larger gains depend on.

Deloitte’s survey also found that 85% of the leaders it studied use different frameworks or timeframes for generative and agentic AI.1 A program can do the same, judging its early slices over months and the agents that act in systems of record over a longer horizon.

What to do next

  1. Agree the four milestones and the evidence for each with finance before the first phase starts, so every steering review reports against them.
  2. Pick a first use-case slice that can run in assist mode by month 3, so the program shows value while the larger controls are still being built.
  3. Set one horizon for read-only and propose-only slices and a longer one for agents that act in systems of record, and report each against its own.

Go deeper

Section 8 of The AI Control Plane Handbook sets out the four phases, how three reference use cases phase in, and the first 90 days. Slides 26 and 27 of the executive deck show the plan and the value at each milestone.

item.title: Every AI claim is a statistical claim
item.description:
Every claim made for an AI system is a statistical claim. An accuracy rate, the savings from a pilot and the share of customers who would use a new agent are all estimates from a sample, and every estimate carries error. In my analysis of a national health survey, one model was 88.7% accurate and still found almost none of the people it was built to find,1 which is the kind of number that statistics exists to catch.

What the plus in AI+ stands for

The site’s name reads as AI, plus the data science, math, statistics and Python behind it. The Visual Handbook’s second chapter sets out how those parts fit: statistics makes sense of data, machine learning learns patterns to predict, and data science combines the two with code and domain knowledge to deliver something useful.2 Statistics asks why a pattern exists, and machine learning asks what comes next.2

Statistics runs through every stage of an AI system, from collecting the right data to measuring whether the system works once it is live.2 A large language model is the clearest case, because it writes by estimating the probability of each possible next word and choosing a likely one.2 When a vendor or a team reports a number about such a system, the number is a statistic, and it can be tested like one.

Questions that test an AI number

Three questions catch most of the ways a number misleads. The survey analysis shows each failure on real data, drawn from 134,897 adults in three years of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.1

Three questions to ask of any AI number, with the failure each one caught in a real analysis
Question What goes wrong without it What it looked like in the survey analysis
Compared with what? An accuracy rate can reflect how rare the outcome is more than how good the model is 88.7% of adults reported no depressive episode, so a model that answered “no” to almost everyone scored 88.7% accuracy
Measured on whom? A sample that over-represents some groups misstates the population Unweighted, 11.29% reported a past-year depressive episode, and weighted to the population the figure was 8.44%
How sure? Ignoring how the sample was drawn makes estimates look more precise than they are Standard errors that respect the survey design were 1.74 to 1.96 times larger, so naive intervals were about half as wide as they should be

The same discipline applies to the model’s own scorecard. A model’s accuracy is a proportion, so it carries a margin of error exactly as a poll does.3 That margin shrinks with the square root of the test set, which means halving it takes four times as many labeled examples.3 A leaderboard number reported without its margin tells you less than it appears to.

None of the three questions needs advanced mathematics. Each needs a habit of asking before a number goes into a decision, and each has a standard answer that a careful analyst can produce.

What to do next

  1. CIO. Ask for the baseline with every accuracy figure, meaning the score of a model that always gives the most common answer.
  2. CTO. Require a margin of error, and the sample behind it, on any model metric that decides whether a system ships.
  3. Analyst. When a sample over-represents some groups, report the figure weighted to the population and say which figure answers the question being asked.

Go deeper

Chapter 2 of Statistics, Data Science and AI: A Visual Handbook maps how statistics, machine learning and data science fit together, with a notebook you can run. The survey analysis works through all three questions on one dataset, with the code behind every figure.

Try it

Choose the right statistical test in four questions puts two of the three questions into practice, “Compared with what?” and “How sure?”, with a decision map and a clinic dataset to test in Colab.

item.title: The same survey says 11.29% or 8.44%
item.description:
The National Survey on Drug Use and Health asked 134,897 adults across 2022 to 2024 about depression, among much else.1 Counted as they answered, 11.29% reported a past-year major depressive episode. Weighted to represent the adult population, the figure is 8.44%.1 Both numbers come from the same people, and only the weighted one describes the country.

Why the weights move the number

The survey is a stratified multistage probability sample. Some groups are over-sampled on purpose, so that estimates for them are precise enough to publish, and every respondent carries a weight saying how many people they represent.2 Young adults are among the over-sampled groups, and they report depression at much higher rates, so the unweighted figure overstates the national rate by about a third.2 A weight undoes the over-sampling. Each young adult counts for fewer people in the population than an older respondent does, so the young adults together count for their true share.

Prevalence among adults, computed two ways from the same respondents1
Measure Unweighted Weighted to the population
Major depressive episode, past year 11.29% 8.44%
Marijuana, past month 19.32% 16.22%
Alcohol, past month 52.65% 51.80%
Cigarettes, past month 14.34% 14.86%

Depression and marijuana move most, and both are concentrated in younger adults, who are over-represented among respondents.1 Cigarette use moves slightly the other way. The direction and the size of the shift depend on who was over-sampled and on how the measure varies across those groups, which is why no rule of thumb replaces computing both.

Who is in the sample matters as much as how each person counts. The three survey years hold 174,407 respondents, and 34,875 of them are aged 12 to 17, who answer a different set of questions and were never asked the adult depression question.1 They are a restriction on the population, so every figure in the analysis describes adults 18 and over.1

The margin of error moves too

The design changes the precision of an estimate as well as the estimate itself. In the same analysis, standard errors that respect the survey’s strata and replicates were 1.74 to 1.96 times larger than naive ones, so a confidence interval built without the design would be roughly half as wide as it should be.1 With a sample this large, no conclusion reversed, but the reported precision would have been wrong.

A margin of error measures precision and nothing more. It can be small on a sample that describes the wrong population, because it says how much an estimate would vary across repeated samples drawn the same way.3 Weighting fixes who the estimate describes, and the design-based margin says how sure you can be.

Survey numbers often lose this context on the way to a slide. A press release quotes one figure, a vendor deck repeats it, and by the time it supports a decision nobody can say whether it was weighted or how wide its interval was.

What to do next

  1. Analyst. Use the survey’s weights and design variables, meaning its strata and its clusters or replicates, for every estimate you publish, and report the design-based margin of error with it.
  2. Analyst. When you show an unweighted figure while exploring the data, label it as describing respondents, and keep it out of any headline.
  3. CIO. Before a survey figure goes into a board paper, ask whether it was weighted and how wide its margin of error is.

Go deeper

The survey analysis computes every descriptive figure both ways, with the R pipeline and a Python notebook behind it. Chapter 74 of the Visual Handbook explains the margin of error and the three things that drive it, and chapter 70 designs and analyzes a survey from start to finish.

item.title: 88.7% accurate and missing almost every case
item.description:
A model built to predict depression from seven survey measures reached 88.7% accuracy on 134,897 adults. At its default setting it flagged 805 of them, although about one in nine had reported a depressive episode, so nearly all of its accuracy came from answering “no”.1 Accuracy alone could not tell that model apart from a useful one.

Accuracy rewards the majority answer

In the analysis sample, 119,664 adults reported no depressive episode and 15,233 did, so a model that always answers “no” is right 88.7% of the time.1 The penalised logistic regression in the analysis matched that score at the default cut-off of 0.50, and its Cohen’s kappa was 0.04, effectively zero.1 Kappa measures agreement beyond what chance alone would produce, which is why it exposed what the accuracy figure hid. A kappa near zero means the model agreed with the truth about as often as chance would, given how rare the outcome is.

The model itself carried real signal. Its AUC of 0.7406 means it ranked a randomly chosen person with depression above a randomly chosen person without it about three times in four.1 The failure was in the decision rule, because the default cut-off of 0.50 sat far above the probabilities the model gives for an outcome this rare. AUC judges the ranking across every possible cut-off, and accuracy judges a single one, which is how the two can disagree so sharply.

One model at five cut-offs, with the same AUC at every one1
Cut-off Depressed adults found Precision Kappa Adults flagged
0.50 2.7% 50.8% 0.040 805 (1%)
0.30 15.8% 37.5% 0.167 6,421 (5%)
0.20 39.0% 29.0% 0.233 20,496 (15%)
0.15 54.2% 24.2% 0.212 34,070 (25%)
0.10 73.5% 19.6% 0.160 56,950 (42%)

Lowering the cut-off to 0.20 finds 39% of the people with depression, at the cost of flagging 15% of everyone for a closer look.1 At that cut-off, 29% of the people flagged have depression, so about seven in ten flags are false alarms.1 That rate suits a quick follow-up question and would be far too high for anything costly or intrusive. Which row is right depends on what happens to a person the model flags, and a cheap follow-up justifies a lower threshold than a costly intervention does.

The outcome is rare enough that people without depression outnumber those with it by 7.86 to 1. Class weighting and resampling, the other standard responses to imbalance, move the model along the same trade-off without adding information, so a team still has to choose where on the curve to sit.1

The Visual Handbook’s chapter on model evaluation shows the same pattern with fraud, where a model that labels every transaction legitimate is 87% accurate and catches no fraud at all.2 Any outcome that is rare enough produces the same illusion, from fraud and equipment failure to an agent’s request that needs a human to review it.

What to do next

  1. CIO. Ask for the base rate with every accuracy figure, and for the share of the cases that matter that the model actually finds.
  2. Analyst. Report recall, precision and kappa beside accuracy for any classifier whose positive class is rare.
  3. Data Scientist. Set the cut-off from the cost of each kind of error, and show the people who will use the model a table like the one above before they choose.

Go deeper

The survey analysis shows the classifier, every cut-off and the code behind them. Chapter 115 of the Visual Handbook covers the confusion matrix, precision and recall, the threshold and the precision-recall curve, with a notebook to run.

Try it

Catch a model that is 88.7% accurate and misses almost every case works through the same checks on card-fraud data, in a visual guide and a notebook that runs in Colab.

item.title: pandas groupby, merge and reshape without surprises
item.description:
Most data analysis in Python runs through three pandas operations: grouping, merging and reshaping. The Visual Handbook’s chapter on Python for data analysis teaches all three on an online store’s order log.1 Each one has a default that can change a result without raising an error, and each has an argument that turns the surprise into a check.

Defaults that change your numbers silently

The code below shows all three on tables small enough to check by eye. It runs as written on pandas 3.0.

import pandas as pd

# 1. groupby leaves out rows whose key is missing
orders = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["East", "West", None], "revenue": [100, 200, 300]})
orders.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum()                # East 100, West 200, and the 300 is gone
orders.groupby("region", dropna=False)["revenue"].sum()  # keeps a missing-region group of 300

# 2. merge multiplies rows when a key repeats where you expected it once
rates = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["East", "East", "West"], "rate": [0.10, 0.20, 0.30]})
orders.merge(rates, on="region", how="left")             # 4 rows from 3 orders
orders.merge(rates, on="region", how="left", validate="many_to_one")  # raises MergeError

# 3. pivot_table averages duplicate cells unless you choose the function
sales = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["A", "A", "B"], "month": ["Jan"] * 3, "units": [10, 30, 5]})
sales.pivot_table(index="store", columns="month", values="units")                 # A shows 20.0
sales.pivot_table(index="store", columns="month", values="units", aggfunc="sum")  # A shows 40

Grouping drops rows whose key is missing by default, so the group totals stop adding up to the column total.2 Pass dropna=False when a missing key should appear as a group of its own, which it usually should in a report.

A merge returns one row for every matching pair of keys. When a lookup table repeats a key that should be unique, every order that matches it is duplicated, and every total built on the result grows with it. The validate argument states the relationship you expect, such as "many_to_one", and raises an error when the data disagrees, while indicator=True adds a column that shows which rows found a match.3

pivot_table combines cells that share an index and a column with the mean by default, so two orders of 10 and 30 units appear as 20.4 Name the function with aggfunc, or use pivot, which raises an error when it meets duplicates.

None of the three raises a warning, because each behaves exactly as documented. The damage shows up later, as a total that no longer matches the source system or a dashboard that drifts after a supplier adds a duplicate row to a reference file.

The pattern repeats across all three operations. pandas picks a reasonable default, the default hides a problem in the data, and one argument brings the problem into view, at the cost of a few characters. A plain check catches what the arguments miss, because comparing the row count and the column total before and after each step shows at once when a step has added or lost data.

What to do next

  1. Analyst. Check that group totals add back to the column total after every groupby, and pass dropna=False whenever missing keys matter.
  2. Developer. Give every merge a validate argument, and use indicator=True while you develop to see which rows failed to match.
  3. Analyst and Developer. Name aggfunc in every pivot_table, and count rows before and after each merge and reshape in your tests.

Go deeper

Chapter 151 of the Visual Handbook covers Python, NumPy, pandas, reshaping and charts across five notebooks, from a raw order log to a finished chart. Its fourth notebook works through groupby, merges, pivot_table and melt on real data.
